# FIG. 3 - Bottom plan view of the vibration device

**View:** Plan view of the underside of the plate, with the tile removed. Pure line work drawn with one uniform thin pen: no hatching, shading, stippling, dashed line, thick line or filled area. No word, digit or label appears, and no border. Each point lies well inside a surface, away from every line and corner, and the three points are far apart.

**Geometry to be drawn**

The sheet holds exactly four closed lines and nothing else, all about one common centre: a large rectangle, a second rectangle within it, a third rectangle within that, and a circle within the third.

Each of the four is drawn once, as a single stroke of even width. No stroke is doubled by a close parallel line beside it, none is drawn as two edges with a core between them, and no shape is repeated as a second outline just inside or just outside itself. Counting every closed line on the finished sheet gives four, three rectangular and one circular. The circle is one thin closed curve with plain white paper inside it, neither a ring nor an annulus nor a hole with a wall, and no smaller circle appears within it.

The three rectangles have square corners and stand well apart from one another: the space between the first and the second, and the space between the second and the third, is a wide expanse of plain white paper, never a hairline gap. The bottom run of the first space and the right run of the second are each deep enough that their middle lies well away from both lines bounding them. The circle is drawn large and stands well inside the third rectangle.

- The extraction opening 30 is the circle at the centre. Identified at the exact centre of that circle, far from its curve.
- The perimeter member 24 is the surface between the second and third rectangles, the loop seen end on. Identified on the right run of that surface, halfway up the height of the sheet, at the point lying halfway between the right line of the second rectangle and the right line of the third, touching neither of those lines and clear of both.
- The second side 16 is the underside surface outside the loop, the plain paper between the first and second rectangles. Identified on the bottom run of that surface, at the mid-width of the sheet, at the point lying halfway between the bottom line of the first rectangle and the bottom line of the second, touching neither of those lines and clear of both.

**Numerals appearing on this figure:** 16, 24, 30

## Numerals shown on this figure

- 16
- 24

**View:** Three-quarter perspective from above and to the front left, onto one large plain tile. Outline line work, no shading, no hatching. Every body except the cable has flat faces and square corners. No word, digit or label appears, and no border.

**Geometry to be drawn**

A large plain tile fills the lower part of the sheet, larger than the device, with no joint line or second tile.

- The base 12 is the lowest part of the assembly, a flat rectangular slab lying on that tile, drawn thick, so its long front side face and the upright face closing its left end each read as a broad plain band with room for a point inside. Every body above stands on the top surface inboard of its edges. Identified within the front side face at the middle of the slab length, halfway between the upper and lower edges of that face and touching neither, not at a corner, on the left end face, or on any body above the slab.
- The vibration device 10 is the whole assembly of slab, blocks, column, handle and cable. Identified at the centre of the left end face of the slab, halfway between its upper and lower edges and halfway between its front and rear edges, so plain paper of that face surrounds the point on every side, never on an edge, a corner, or a body above the slab.

- The duct 32 is an upright rectangular column rising from the middle of the slab, tall and narrow, with plain paper at each side. Identified on its flat front face at mid-height.
- The air-extraction mechanism 20 is a second rectangular block on top of that column, lifted clear of the slab and touching it nowhere. Identified on its flat right-hand face at mid-height.
- The fasteners 54 are a row of square bolt heads standing on the slab in front of the motor block, each a small block with a flat top tall enough to read as a body. Identified at the centre of the flat top of the one nearest the front left, above the slab surface.

# FIG. 3 - Bottom plan view of the vibration device

**View:** Plan view of the underside of the plate, with the tile removed. Pure line work drawn with one uniform thin pen: no hatching, shading, stippling, dashed line, thick line or filled area. No word, digit or label appears, and no border. Each point lies well inside a surface, away from every line and corner, and the three points are far apart.

**Geometry to be drawn**

The sheet holds exactly four closed lines and nothing else, all about one common centre: a large rectangle, a second rectangle within it, a third rectangle within that, and a circle within the third.

Each of the four is drawn once, as a single stroke of even width. No stroke is doubled by a close parallel line beside it, none is drawn as two edges with a core between them, and no shape is repeated as a second outline just inside or just outside itself. Counting every closed line on the finished sheet gives four, three rectangular and one circular. The circle is one thin closed curve with plain white paper inside it, neither a ring nor an annulus nor a hole with a wall, and no smaller circle appears within it.

The three rectangles have square corners and stand well apart from one another: the space between the first and the second, and the space between the second and the third, is a wide expanse of plain white paper, never a hairline gap. The left run of the first space and the right run of the second are each broad enough that their middle lies well away from both lines bounding them, with room for a point on open paper between those lines. The circle is drawn large and stands well inside the third rectangle.

- The extraction opening 30 is the circle at the centre. Identified at the exact centre of that circle, far from its curve.
- The perimeter member 24 is the surface between the second and third rectangles, the loop seen end on. Identified on the right run of that surface, halfway up the height of the sheet, at the point lying halfway between the right line of the second rectangle and the right line of the third, touching neither of those lines and clear of both.
- The second side 16 is the underside surface outside the loop, the plain paper between the first and second rectangles. Identified on the left run of that surface, level with the height of the centre of the circle, at the point lying halfway between the left line of the first rectangle and the left line of the second, so that blank paper of equal depth stands to the left and to the right of the point. The point sits on open paper only: it is not on the first rectangle, not on the second rectangle, not on any horizontal or vertical drawn line, and not within reach of a corner.

Both failing sheets are repaired; nothing else in the application was touched.

**FIG. 1, numeral 10** — the endpoint kept landing on the top-front-left corner vertex of the base slab because the old target ("the open stretch of the slab top surface between the column and the handle") is a foreshortened band in perspective, and an assembly numeral naturally drifts to the extreme corner of the whole device. I moved the target to a bounded, four-sided face: the upright left end face of the slab, with the point at its centre, halfway between upper and lower edges and halfway between front and rear edges, explicitly off every edge and corner. This also matches the target the endpoint stage reported as required, and it mirrors the already certified FIG. 5, where numeral 10 sits inside a slab side face and passed. To keep that face open I made the motor block set back from the left end as well as the front edge, and I moved numeral 12's own callout language to exclude the left end face so the two slab callouts cannot be confused (12 stays at mid-length of the front side face, half a slab length away).

**FIG. 3, numeral 16** — the chooser snapped to y=900 (outer rectangle bottom line) and then y=750 (middle rectangle bottom line), i.e. it kept selecting the bounding lines of the bottom margin rather than the paper between them, even after the brief already said "halfway between". I moved the callout to a fresh run, the left margin between the first and second rectangles at the height of the circle's centre, restated the midpoint condition as equal blank paper left and right of the point, and added a flat exclusion that the point is on open paper only. The geometry paragraph now names the left run of the outer space (instead of the bottom run) as the one that must be broad enough to hold a point clear of both bounding lines. Numeral 24 stays on the right run and 30 at the circle centre, so the three points remain far apart and on opposite sides of the sheet.

Both edited briefs are back under the 2800 character cap (FIG. 1 at 2794, FIG. 3 at 2744); I trimmed redundant wording elsewhere in FIG. 1 rather than dropping any geometry or topology constraint that earlier gates rely on. The nine text sections, all claims, the 22 numeral definitions, the five-figure plan, and the numeral-to-sheet assignments are unchanged, as are FIG. 2, FIG. 4, and FIG. 5.

content.text:
Repaired FIG. 1, the only failing sheet.

**Root cause of the endpoint failures (10 and 12):** both points were required to sit inside the thickness faces of the base slab, and the renderer draws that slab thin, so the front side face and the left end face are shallow bands. The rejections confirm it: 10 at (203, 655) fell on blank paper beside the slab or near the top edge of the end face, and 12 at (500, 705) fell on the bottom edge of the front face. Only one slab face can be relied on to hold a point, so I stopped asking for two.

- **Numeral 10** now uses the target that is already certified on FIG. 5: within the front side face at the middle of the slab length, halfway between its upper and lower edges, with paper of the face above and below the point, and explicitly not on the top surface, the tile, an edge, or a corner. The left end face is no longer used by any numeral.
- **Numeral 12** moves to the base's own top surface, which is a broad quadrilateral rather than a thin band, and is located by two midpoints so the placement is determinate: in the open stretch between the duct column and the handle, midway between the front and rear top edges and midway between the column and the nearer handle upright. Pointing the base numeral at the base's top surface is also the more natural reading, and it separates 10 and 12 in two different planes and at different positions along the slab.
- The base entry now requires the slab to be drawn large and thick so the front face is deep enough to take a point well inside it, using the same wording that produced a passing sheet in FIG. 5.
- **Numeral 54** failed because the bolt heads render too small to hold a certified point. The heads are now drawn large and set apart, each with a flat top face that reads as a clear quadrilateral, and the point sits at the centre of that face away from its edges. I also moved them from "a row in front of the motor block" to "around the foot of the motor block", which matches the detailed description's "fasteners 54 spaced around its foot" more exactly.
- **Numeral 50** had no terminal dot on its leader. The cable's mid-run is now specified as an unbroken sweep through open paper above the slab, clear of the handle and every other body, with the identified point at the middle of that open sweep where plain paper lies each side of it and no other line comes near, so the dot lands on clear ground instead of merging with adjacent line work.

FIG. 2, FIG. 3, FIG. 4, and FIG. 5 are untouched, as are all nine text sections, the claims, the 22-entry numeral table, the Brief Description of the Drawings, and FIG. 1's numeral membership (10, 12, 18, 20, 32, 44, 50, 54). The brief is 2796 characters, within the cap.

input.summary: Repaired FIG. 1, the only sheet reported as failing. Numeral 10 moved to the front side face of the base slab at the middle of its length (the target already certified on FIG. 5), numeral 12 moved to the base's broad top surface in the open stretch between the duct column and the handle, located by two midpoints, so neither point depends on a shallow slab thickness face that the renderer keeps drawing too thin. The base entry now requires the slab to be drawn large and thick so the front face is deep enough to hold a point well inside it. Fastener heads are now drawn large and set apart, around the foot of the motor block as the detailed description recites, with the point at the centre of a flat top face that reads as a clear quadrilateral. The cable's mid-run is now an unbroken sweep through open paper above the slab, clear of the handle and every other body, with the identified point where plain paper lies each side of it so the terminal dot lands on clear ground. FIG. 2 through FIG. 5, all nine text sections, the claims, the numeral table, the drawing descriptions, and FIG. 1's numeral membership are unchanged; the brief is 2796 characters.
reasoning: The two endpoint rejections on FIG. 1 shared one cause: numerals 10 and 12 both had to sit inside thickness faces of the base slab, and the rendered slab is thin. The reported coordinates prove it, 10 at (203, 655) on blank paper beside the slab or crowding the top edge of the end face, and 12 at (500, 705) sitting on the bottom edge of the front face. No amount of extra wording makes a shallow band hold a certifiable point, so I reduced the sheet to one thickness-face target instead of two.

Numeral 10 took the front side face because that is the exact target shape already certified on FIG. 5, where numeral 10 sits inside the near side face of the slab and passed. Reusing a proven target is more reliable than inventing a third location.

Numeral 12 moved to the base's top surface, which is a broad quadrilateral in this perspective rather than a band. I located it by two independent midpoints, midway between the front and rear top edges and midway between the column and the nearer handle upright, because that construction is what made the FIG. 3 repair converge. It also reads better: the base numeral now points at the base's own top surface.

Separating the two points into different planes and different positions along the slab length removes the earlier risk of a reviewer confusing them, which was a live concern while 10 and 12 sat on two faces meeting at the same vertical edge. Numeral 10 on FIG. 1 was the only remaining failure, and it was still tied to the slab's front vertical face: at (525, 753) the point landed on a horizontal edge of that face, the same shallow-band problem that produced the previous two rejections there.

**What changed in `figures/FIG-1-PERSPECTIVE-VIEW-OF-THE-VIBRATION-DEVICE-IN-USE.md`:**

- **Numeral 10** no longer uses any thickness face of the slab. It now sits on the top surface of the base, in the open bay between the motor block and the duct column, fixed by two midpoints (midway between the front and rear top edges, midway between the motor block and the column) and explicitly clear of the bolt heads and of every edge and corner. That surface is the one region on this sheet already proven to hold a certified point, since numeral 12 passed there on the last render. A point on the slab's top surface is a point on the assembly, which is what numeral 10 designates.
- **Numeral 12** keeps its certified location, the open bay between the column and the handle, with the same two-midpoint construction. Its sentence now names that bay explicitly rather than referring back, so the two bays cannot be confused: 10 is left of the column, 12 is right of it.
- The base entry now recites the two open bays of the top surface, and I dropped the requirement that the front side face be deep enough to take a point, since no numeral targets that face any more. That removes a rendering constraint the drawing no longer needs.
- **Fasteners 54** are drawn close around the foot of the motor block, so the bay used by numeral 10 stays open. Their own endpoint, which passed, is unchanged.
- Entries for 18, 20, 32, 44 and 50 are unchanged apart from two word-level trims made to hold the brief at 2795 characters.

FIG. 2 through FIG. 5 are untouched, as are the nine text sections, the claims, the 22-entry numeral table, the Brief Description of the Drawings, and FIG. 1's numeral membership (10, 12, 18, 20, 32, 44, 50, 54).

Numeral 10 now sits on the base's top surface in the open bay between the motor block and the duct column, located by two midpoints and kept clear of the bolt heads and of every edge and corner. Numeral 12 keeps its certified location in the bay between the column and the handle, its sentence now naming that bay explicitly so the two bays cannot be confused. The base entry recites both open bays and no longer demands a front side face deep enough to take a point, a constraint no numeral needs now. Fasteners are drawn close around the motor foot so the bay used by numeral 10 stays open. FIG. 2 through FIG. 5, all nine text sections, the claims, the numeral table, the drawing descriptions, and FIG. 1's numeral membership are unchanged; the brief is 2795 characters.
reasoning: Numeral 10 has now been rejected three times on the slab's thickness faces: on the left end face it fell on blank paper and near the top edge, and on the front side face it fell on the bottom edge and then, at (525, 753), on a horizontal edge again. The renderer draws the slab as a thin plate in this crowded perspective, so its vertical faces are shallow bands whose interior is only a few pixels deep. I stopped writing a target that depends on that band.

The top surface of the base is the one region on this sheet with demonstrated capacity to hold a certified point: numeral 12 passed there on the last render using a two-midpoint construction. I gave numeral 10 the same construction in the adjacent bay, so the placement is determinate rather than left to judgement about what counts as 'well inside'.

Numeral 10 designates the whole assembly, which the entry defines as slab, blocks, column, handle and cable, so a point on the slab's top surface lies within the thing the numeral names. That keeps the leader honest while using the largest available region.

The two bays of the top surface are now named by the bodies that bound them, one between the motor block and the column for 10 and one between the column and the handle for 12, and 12's sentence names its bay outright instead of referring back to the preceding clause. The points are on opposite sides of the duct column, which separates them along the slab and prevents a reviewer from reading either point into the other's region.

I deleted the requirement that the front side face be a band deep enough to take a point well inside it. No numeral targets that face any more, so it was an invented rendering constraint with nothing depending on it, and dropping it also freed the characters the new endpoint sentences needed.

The fasteners now stand close around the foot of the motor block rather than merely around it, so the bay between the motor block and the column stays clear for numeral 10's point. Their own endpoint on the flat top face passed last round and is unchanged.

Everything that passed was left alone except two word-level trims in the entries for the base and the air-extraction block, needed to hold the file at or below the 2800 character cap. No geometry, topology, or line-count constraint that earlier OCR, semantic, and topology gates rely on was removed.

No file in draft/ was touched. The review raised no text finding, and the numeral table, Brief Description of the Drawings, and detailed description already match the repaired brief because only endpoint locations changed, not what the figure shows.

**Geometry to be drawn**

A large plain tile fills the lower sheet, larger than the device, with no joint line or second tile.

- The base 12 is a flat rectangular slab lying on that tile, drawn large and of visible thickness, its top surface a broad quadrilateral. Bodies above stand on it inboard of its edges, leaving two open stretches of it, one between the motor block and the column, one between the column and the handle. Identified in the open stretch between the column and the handle, midway between the front and rear top edges and midway between the column and the nearer handle upright.

- The air-extraction mechanism 20 is a rectangular block on top of that column, clear of the slab. Identified on its flat right-hand face at mid-height.

Numeral 10 on FIG. 1 was the only failure, and the report says it stayed inside a coordinate cluster that has already been rejected. Every target tried so far sat on or beside the base slab, in the band of the sheet around the rejected points (203, 655), (500, 705) and (525, 753), so the fix had to put its pixels somewhere else on the sheet.

**What changed in `figures/FIG-1-PERSPECTIVE-VIEW-OF-THE-VIBRATION-DEVICE-IN-USE.md`:**

- **Numeral 10** now lands on the flat top face of the upper block, the highest surface of the assembly, at the centre of that face by two midpoints, on plain paper of the face and touching no edge, corner or other body. That block stands high above the slab and clear of it, so the endpoint falls well away from the rejected slab-level cluster, and the top face is a broad horizontal quadrilateral with blank paper above it rather than a foreshortened band.
- **Numeral 20** keeps its certified endpoint on the right-hand face of that block at mid-height, now stated as below the top face, so the two points sit on different planes of the block and cannot be read into each other's region. The block's entry also requires the top face to be drawn broad and open.
- **Numeral 12** returns to the single open stretch of slab top surface between the column and the handle, with the two-midpoint construction that was certified last round. The second bay between the motor block and the column is no longer reserved, since nothing targets it now.
- **Fasteners 54, handle 44, motor 18, duct 32 and supply 50** are unchanged apart from wording trims needed to hold the brief at 2793 characters.

FIG. 2 through FIG. 5, the nine text sections, the claims, the 22-entry numeral table, the Brief Description of the Drawings, and FIG. 1's numeral membership (10, 12, 18, 20, 32, 44, 50, 54) are untouched.

input.summary: Fixed the single remaining failure, numeral 10 on FIG. 1, which stayed inside an already rejected coordinate cluster. Its target moved from the base slab to the flat top face of the upper block, the highest surface of the assembly, located at the centre of that face by two midpoints and kept off every edge, corner and other body. That places its pixels high above the slab, far from the rejected cluster around the slab faces. The upper block entry now requires that top face to be drawn broad and open with blank paper above it, and numeral 20 keeps its certified right-hand face endpoint, now stated as below the top face so the two points sit on different planes. Numeral 12 returns to the single certified bay of slab top surface between the column and the handle. FIG. 2 through FIG. 5, all nine text sections, the claims, the numeral table, the drawing descriptions, and FIG. 1's numeral membership are unchanged; the brief is 2793 characters.
reasoning: The report gave the operative fact: numeral 10 is not merely misplaced, it keeps resolving into a coordinate cluster that has already been rejected, so any further wording change aimed at the same part of the sheet would be re-proposed at blocked coordinates. Every target tried so far, the left end face, the front side face twice, and the slab top surface bay, lies in the same band of the sheet as the rejected points (203, 655), (500, 705) and (525, 753). The target had to move in pixel space, not just in prose.

The upper block is the only large body whose surfaces sit well outside that band: it stands on top of the duct column, clear of the slab, so its top face is high on the sheet. Its top face is also a broad horizontal quadrilateral rather than a foreshortened band, which is the failure mode that defeated all three slab-face attempts.
